info.bio: Woodrow Wilson Guthrie (Okemah, Oklahoma, 14 de julio de 1912 – Nueva York, 3 de octubre de 1967), conocido como Woody Guthrie, fue un prolífico e influyente músico folk estadounidense, gran identificación con la gente común, los pobres y los oprimidos, así como por su odio al fascismo y la explotación. su canción «This Land Is Your Land»inspirada en sus experiencias viajando por todos los Estados Unidos. En los últimos versos de la canción, Guthrie protestaba contra las desigualdades sociales.

scenes.name: Antecedentes (1892-1950)
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Antes del rock'n'roll: Tin Pan Alley, los primeros discos de blues (Mamie Smith) y de «old-time music», el yodel de Jimmie Rodgers, el crooning de Bing Crosby, el boogie-woogie, el jump blues de Louis Jordan (nacimiento de facto del rhythm'n'blues), la guitarra jazzística de T-Bone Walker, Woody Guthrie como primer gran cantautor y la exótica de Les Baxter. En paralelo, la vanguardia clásica (Russolo, Satie, Varèse, Cage, Schaeffer) anticipa el ruido, el ambient y la electrónica.

podcast.title: Journey to California (1936)
podcast.body: After years of odd jobs in Oklahoma and Texas, Guthrie traveled to California in 1936 in search of work, where he connected with his cousin, Jack Guthrie. "But then in 1936 he travelled out to California in search of work."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Anti-Fascist Guitar Message
podcast.body: Woody Guthrie famously inscribed the phrase "This Machine Kills Fascists" on his guitar, turning his instrument into a symbol of his political activism. He was persecuted and censored by the system, blacklisted as a communist, and dedicated his career to performing at strikes and writing hundreds of anti-establishment songs, embodying a "punk" attitude before the genre existed. "con su famosa guitarra en la que escribió Dismachin Kill's Fasits, fue perseguido y censurado por el sistema, vetado por comunista, tocó en vuelgas y escribió cientos de canciones contra el sistema, un punk en todas reglas y amplificadores."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: El punk existía antes de Sex Pistols (y era algo salvaje)

podcast.title: Communist Sympathies
podcast.body: Guthrie associated with members of the Communist Party but apparently never formally joined, being more interested in supporting "victims against the bullies" than Marxist theory. He initially adopted the communist stance on World War II as a capitalist fight until Russia joined, then became an anti-fascist. "He started hanging around with members of the Communist Party, though he apparently never joined."

podcast.title: Early Career as Country Singer
podcast.body: He began his career as a country singer, drawing inspiration from 1920s greats like The Carter Family and Jimmie Rodgers. "Guthrie had started out as a country singer, singing songs inspired by the Carter family, Jimmy Rogers, and other 1920s greats."

podcast.title: Friend of Pete Seeger
podcast.body: Woody Guthrie was friends with Pete Seeger in the 1940s. "He had been friends with both Woody Guthrie and Lead Belly in the 40s."

podcast.title: Huntington's Disease
podcast.body: By January 1961, Guthrie was severely ill with Huntington's disease, a genetic disorder that also claimed his mother. The disease caused dementia, spasmodic movements, and loss of body control. He had been in a psychiatric hospital since 1956, with Sunday visits to family. "Guthrie was, by this time, severely ill. He had Huntington's disease, a truly awful genetic disorder that had also killed his mother."

podcast.title: Labeled as Communist (1930s-1940s)
podcast.body: During the 1930s and 1940s, Woody Guthrie utilized folk music as a vehicle to disseminate messages that led to him being labeled as a communist. "In the 30s and 40s, Woody got three and Pete Seeger used folk music to spread messages that had them labeled as communists."

podcast.title: Left-Wing Activism
podcast.body: Guthrie participated in left-wing activism, which Pete Seeger dedicated his later career to. "he dedicated his later career to the same kind of left-wing activism the Guthrie had taken part in."

podcast.title: Mentorship of Ramblin' Jack Elliott
podcast.body: Guthrie was a mentor and "apprentice master" to Ramblin' Jack Elliott, who lived with him and learned everything from him, enabling Elliott to become a significant figure in the British folk and skiffle scenes. "Elliott at Napaas, the son of a surgeon, had become Ramblin Jack the singing in Cowboy, and had been an apprentice of Guthrie, living with him and learning everything from him"

podcast.title: Most Important Folk Singer
podcast.body: Guthrie was considered the most important of the left-wing folk singers centered in Armanac House, influencing groups like The Armanac Singers and The Weavers. "And Guthrie had been the most most important of all of them."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Move to New York
podcast.body: Losing his newspaper job due to his employer's stronger anti-fascist views, Guthrie moved to New York and joined a group of left-wing intellectuals and folk singers, including Alan Lomax, Pete Seeger, and Lead Belly, at Armanac House in Greenwich Village. "Guthrie lost his newspaper job, and he decided to move across the country to New York, where he hooked up with a group of left-wing intellectuals and folk singers"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Pivotal in American Folk Music
podcast.body: Woody Guthrie was a pivotal figure in the development of American folk music in the 1930s, particularly noted for politicizing the genre. "Guthrie is someone we've only mentioned in passing so far, but he was pivotal in the development of American folk music in the 1930s, and in particular he was important in the politicisation of that music."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Radicalization and Newspaper Work
podcast.body: After Lefty Lou left, the left-wing owner of their radio station, who also ran a left-wing newspaper, hired Guthrie to write columns about the plight of Oki migrants. Spending time with these impoverished and discriminated people radicalized Guthrie. "Guthrie went and spent time with those people, and his shock at the poverty they were living in and the discrimination they were suffering seems to have radicalised him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Skiffle Repertoire
podcast.body: His songs were a primary component of the repertoire for skiffle groups, alongside those of Lead Belly and Big Bill Broonzy. "a repertoire that was made up primarily of songs by Lead Belly, Woody Guthrie and Big Bill Brunze."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: The Oki and Woody Show
podcast.body: Woody and his cousin Jack Guthrie performed together with a group called the Beverly Hillbillies and had their own radio show called "The Oki and Woody Show," which was not successful. "They performed with a group called the Beverly Hill Belize and got their own radio show, the Oki and Woody show, but it wasn't successful"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: The Woody and Lefty Act
podcast.body: After Jack Guthrie quit, Woody continued performing with Maxine Christman, known as Lefty Lou from Old Mizzou. Their duo became "hugely popular" until Lefty quit due to failing health, which indirectly benefited Guthrie's career. "The Woody and Lefty act became hugely popular, but Lefty eventually also quit due to her health failing."

xref.title: Challenged the Status Quo
xref.body: Bob Dylan emerged in the wake of the folk movement pioneered by Woody Guthrie and Pete Seeger. He was notable for his willingness to directly challenge and critique the prevailing social and political conditions of his time. "The folk movement that came in their wake gave us people like Bob Dylan, who had no trouble poking the status quo in the eye."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Labeled as Communist (1930s-1940s)
xref.body: Pete Seeger, along with Woody Guthrie, used folk music in the 1930s and 1940s to spread messages that resulted in both of them being labeled as communists. His membership in the American Communist Party later caused him significant difficulties. "Seeger was a member of the American Communist Party, and that's something that caused him all sorts of headaches later."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
